title: Microfluidic-based Electrotaxis for On-demand Quantitative Analysis of Caenorhabditis elegans' Locomotion
protocol: Bathe a 3 in. silicon wafer in acetone for 30 sec.
Rinse the wafer with methanol for 30 sec.
Rinse the wafer with dH2O water for 5 min.
Dry the wafer's surface with a N2 blow gun.
Heat the wafer on a hot plate at 140 °C for 2 min.
Plasma oxidize the silicon wafer surface (1 min, 50 W).
Spin-coat the wafer's surface with 3 ml SU-8 100 photoresist (40 sec; 1,750 rpm).
Pre-bake the coated wafer on a hot plate at 65 °C for 10 min.
Ramp the temperature up to 95 °C over 2 min and maintain for an additional 1 hr.
Align a photomask containing the desired channel design.
Expose the resist to 550-600 mJ/cm² of UV light (350-400 nm).
Post-bake the wafer on a hot plate at 65 °C for 1 min and 95 °C for 10 min, ramping temperature as before.
Immerse the wafer in SU-8 developer solution for 10-15 min.
Rinse with isopropanol to check completion of development.
Pour 20 ml of PDMS prepolymer into the master mold dish.
Pour 15 ml of PDMS prepolymer into the second dish.
Gently press on the wafers with a disposable wooden applicator to eliminate air pockets underneath them.
Cover both dishes and set aside for a day to cure.
Alternatively, remove air bubbles from the PDMS using a vacuum degasifier.
Place the dishes on a hot plate at 80 °C for 2 hours.
Remove the foil and peel the cured PDMS from the wafers.
Punch fluid access ports at both ends of the channel using the Harris Uni-Core (2.5 mm).
Cut the channel and blank PDMS into similarly sized strips.
Load the channel, the blank PDMS strip, and a glass slide (75×25 mm²) into a plasma oxidizer.
Expose to oxygen plasma for 40 seconds at 40 W power.
Stick the channel piece and glass slide to opposite sides of the blank strip.
Set aside the assembly for 2 hours to complete bonding.
Place the assembly onto a hot plate at 120 °C.
Attach plastic tubing (inner diameter 1/32", outer diameter 3/32") to each punched reservoir.
Affix fluidic plastic connectors or commercially available fittings to one or both tubes to allow syringe attachment.
Insert 3" lengths of 22 gauge insulated copper wire into each reservoir between the inlet tube and the channel.
Secure the wires with PDMS prepolymer.
Place the microchannel on the stage of a microscope with a mounted camera connected to a monitor.
Connect the power supply or amplifier's output wires to the microchannel's electrodes.
Attach the microchannel's output tube to a disposable syringe.
Submerge the mouth of the inlet tube in M9 physiological buffer and gently aspire liquid into the channel by applying a negative pressure inside the syringe.
Level both tubes to the same height to prevent hydrostatically driven flow.
Apply a DC voltage to the channel and ensure that resistance is around 0.6 MΩ.
Disconnect the syringe from the tube when the inlet and outlet tubes are filled with M9.
Load worms from a diluted suspension into the channel.
Disconnect the syringe and hydrostatically manipulate the flow by adjusting the tubes' relative height.
Place a worm in the center of the channel using this method.
Lay both tubes flat at the same elevation.
Set the power supply to 4-12 V/cm for L3 stage animals, 4-10 V/cm for L4s, and 2-4 V/cm for young adults.
Activate the electric signal and allow 1 min of pre-exposure.
Record using a camera after the acclimatization period.
Remove all liquid (and worms) from the channel when the experiment is finished.
Rinse the channel with dH2O.
Place the device on a hot plate at 125 °C to dry.
